foodDescription: Porto’s “little Frenchwoman”: bread layered with ham, sausage, and steak, covered in melted cheese and a spiced tomato and beer sauce, usually with fries. Said to be a 1950s take on the croque-monsieur. One is a meal.

Tripe stewed with white beans, sausage, and cumin. The story goes that in 1415 Porto gave its meat to the fleet sailing to take Ceuta and kept the offal, which is why people here are still called tripeiros, “tripe-eaters.”

foodEnglishName: Baked salt cod with potatoes and egg
foodDescription: Flaked salt cod baked with sliced potatoes, onions, and olive oil, topped with boiled egg and olives. Created in Porto in the late 1800s by José Luís Gomes de Sá, the son of a cod merchant.
A thin sausage and cheese in a long, crisp, pressed roll, cut into bites and brushed with spicy sauce. Gazela, a narrow bar near São Bento station, is the famous place for them.
Slow-roasted pork leg sliced into a soft roll with its juices, often with runny sheep’s cheese from the Serra da Estrela mountains. Casa Guedes, on Praça dos Poveiros, is known for it.
Thin pork cutlets simmered in garlic, white wine, and paprika and tucked into a roll. Eaten standing at the counter with a small beer; Conga, on Rua do Bonjardim, has served them for decades.
A smooth potato soup with ribbons of finely shredded kale and a slice of chouriço sausage. It comes from the Minho, the region north of Porto, and is eaten all night at the São João festival in June.
Whole sardines grilled over charcoal and eaten on bread, which soaks up the oil. Best from June to September, when the fish are fattest, and everywhere on the night of São João.

Fresh fish grilled on charcoal grills set out on the street in Matosinhos, Porto’s fishing harbor, a short metro ride away. Restaurants on Rua Heróis de França sell it by weight, with boiled potatoes and salad.
A dense, dark, slightly sweet bread of corn and rye, baked for hours in wood ovens in Avintes, a village across the river in Gaia. Often eaten with sardines or caldo verde.

Sweet wine from the Douro valley, fortified with grape brandy and aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river. White port with tonic is a local aperitif; tawny and ruby come after dinner.
Light, young, slightly fizzy wine from the Minho region north of Porto. The “green” means young, not the color: it comes in white, red, and rosé. Cheap, cold, and good with seafood.
What Porto calls an espresso, after the Italian La Cimbali machines that brought espresso to the city. In Lisbon the same coffee is a bica; ask for a “café” anywhere and you get one too.
A small glass of draft beer in Porto; in Lisbon it’s an imperial. Here it will usually be Super Bock, brewed just outside the city in Leça do Balio.
